metadata.file_name: 21. Koo & Yoo. (2025). Teachers’ team innovativeness in TALIS 2018: An empirical and simulation study using glmmLasso for multilevel data.pdf
metadata.title: Teachers’ team innovativeness in TALIS 2018: An empirical and simulation study using glmmLasso for multilevel data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 microdata for Korean middle school teachers and principals, with teachers nested within schools (multilevel structure). In data cleaning, the authors explicitly removed weighting-related variables (e.g., SCHWGT) from the predictor set, but they do not state whether complex survey weights were applied in estimation. The modeling approach (glmmLasso, LASSO, elastic net) is a penalized regression framework that is not described as weight-aware, so the manuscript provides insufficient detail to confirm whether sampling weights were used for population-representative inference. Missingness was handled via k-nearest neighbors imputation using Gower distance on complete observations, after excluding variables with ≥20% missingness.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a TALIS scale score (T3TEAM) derived from confirmatory factor analysis of Likert items, not a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported as k-nearest neighbors imputation using Gower distance, so the paper does not omit the missing-data strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 Korean middle school teacher and principal responses. The analytic dataset was constructed by removing irrelevant variables (including IDs and weighting/administration variables such as SCHWGT and VERSION), excluding TALIS variables with ≥20% missingness, dummy-coding categorical items (and treating multi-category items as grouped dummy variables), merging teacher and principal datasets, and retaining 2895 teachers and 163 principals with 571 explanatory variables. Missing values in the remaining predictors were imputed using k-nearest neighbors with Gower distance (k=25) based on 644 complete observations.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teachers can rely on each other
Lack of employer support for PD

main_findings.performance_metrics: Empirical Study I: RMSE distributions for glmmLasso, LASSO, and elastic net had overlapping 95% confidence intervals (exact RMSE values not reported in the abstract; Table 2 reports RMSE mean ~1.775–1.792 with overlapping CIs). glmmLasso selected fewer variables with lower variability (mean selected ~30.48, SD=9.98) versus LASSO (~92.41, SD=133.82) and elastic net (~111.01, SD=190.61).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (KOR) the study leveraged joint activities across classes, work with other teachers, team conferences, teacher self-efficacy for motivating low-interest students, and shared beliefs about teaching to predict teachers’ team innovativeness (T3TEAM), finding that most selected predictors showed positive associations while shared responsibility for school issues (TT3G48D) showed a negative association. This indicates that school policies should prioritize structured teacher collaboration and supportive, innovation-friendly school cultures, while carefully considering how “shared responsibility” is implemented so it does not undermine teachers’ perceived ownership of innovation.

main_findings.target_variable: Predictive accuracy and variable selection for teachers’ team innovativeness
main_findings.performance_metrics: Simulation Study II: RMSE means were very similar across methods (glmmLasso mean ~2.154; LASSO ~2.135; elastic net ~2.136) with overlapping 95% CIs (Table 7). glmmLasso selected substantially fewer variables (mean ~11.92, SD=1.08) than LASSO (~42.24, SD=13.01) and elastic net (~44.59, SD=12.31) (Table 8). Variable-selection quality: at the 75% threshold, glmmLasso had IC1=0 for true predictors and IC2=1 false positive at level-2; LASSO/elastic net had larger IC2 at level-2 (IC2=6 and 7, respectively).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using a TALIS 2018–structured simulation with nested teachers within schools (ICC≈0.09), the study leveraged level-1 and level-2 predictor signals under a multilevel random-effects data-generating process to evaluate predictive accuracy and variable selection, finding that glmmLasso achieved comparable RMSE to LASSO/elastic net while selecting a smaller, more accurate set of true predictors (especially at the school level). This indicates that penalized multilevel modeling can improve interpretability and reduce false-positive policy targets when analyzing nested large-scale education data, even when predictive accuracy differences are modest.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 Korean middle school teachers and principals (2895 teachers; 163 principals) using teachers’ team innovativeness (T3TEAM) as a continuous scale score derived from four Likert items. For prediction and variable selection, the authors compare glmmLasso (penalized GLMM) against LASSO and elastic net, using repeated train/test splitting (7:3) and RMSE as the predictive error. In the empirical analysis, RMSE distributions across methods overlap (95% CIs), but glmmLasso is more parsimonious and stable, selecting far fewer predictors on average (≈30.48 vs ≈92.41 and ≈111.01). In simulation (ICC≈0.09), glmmLasso again shows similar RMSE (≈2.154) while substantially improving variable-selection accuracy at level-2 (IC2=1 vs IC2=6–7). A key limitation is that the manuscript does not clearly report whether TALIS sampling weights were applied in estimation, and the negative association for shared responsibility is correlational rather than causal.
